title: Philosophy: Big Ideas · Episode 1
chapters: Diogenes: the philosopher who lived in a jar
Epicurus: the surprising philosophy of pleasure
Eastern philosophy: sages of India and China

units.t: Philosophy: Big Ideas. Episode one.
In this episode: Diogenes: the philosopher who lived in a jar, Epicurus: the surprising philosophy of pleasure, The Socratic method and Eastern philosophy: sages of India and China.
Part one. Diogenes: the philosopher who lived in a jar.
He slept in a storage jar, carried a lamp in daylight and reportedly told Alexander the Great to get out of his sunlight.
Behind the stunts was a serious idea about what we really need.
Deface the currency.
Diogenes was born around 412 BC in Sinope, a Greek trading city on the Black Sea.
Almost everything we know comes from stories gathered centuries later, especially by the biographer Diogenes Laertius, so many details are legend.
By these accounts, Diogenes or his father, who was in charge of the city's money, was caught defacing the coinage, and Diogenes was exiled.
He turned the incident into a motto: deface the currency.
He meant challenging the false values society stamps onto things, such as wealth, status, fashion and good manners.
Arriving in Athens, he set about testing which values were genuine and which were counterfeit.
Life in a jar.
In Athens, Diogenes lived in a large ceramic storage jar near the marketplace.
He owned a cloak, a staff and a bag, and little else.
One story says he had a drinking cup until he saw a boy drinking from his cupped hands.
He threw the cup away, declaring that a child had beaten him in simplicity.
He ate, slept and did everything else in public, scandalising respectable citizens.
They called him kyon, meaning dog.
He embraced the insult, and his followers became known as Cynics, from the Greek for doglike.
Their aim was to live according to nature, free of needless wants.
Lamp and sunlight.
Diogenes was a performer as much as a thinker.
He reportedly walked the streets in daylight with a lit lamp, saying he was looking for a human being, meaning an honest one.
When Plato defined a human as a featherless creature that walks on two legs, Diogenes supposedly plucked a chicken and announced, 'Here is Plato's human.'
In the most famous tale, Alexander the Great found him lying in the sun in Corinth and asked if he could do anything for him.
'Yes,' said Diogenes, 'stand out of my sunlight.'
Alexander reportedly said that if he were not Alexander, he would wish to be Diogenes.
Historians cannot confirm the meeting.
Its point still strikes: someone who wants nothing cannot be bribed, flattered or threatened.
Citizen of the world.
Asked where he came from, Diogenes reportedly said he was a kosmopolites, a citizen of the world, the origin of our word cosmopolitan.
In ancient Greece this was radical: identity was bound to one's city, and exile was among the worst punishments.
If what matters is living well according to nature, Diogenes implied, the borders and customs of any one city are secondary.
The idea travelled.
Crates of Thebes, his most important follower, gave away a fortune to live as a Cynic.
He married Hipparchia, a wealthy woman who chose that life and became one of the few women philosophers of ancient Greece whose name survives.
Crates taught Zeno, founder of the Stoics, who developed the idea into all humans belonging to one community of reason.
What he still teaches.
Diogenes died in Corinth, traditionally in 323 BC, the same year as Alexander, though the dates are uncertain.
The Cynics were street philosophers with no building or fixed curriculum.
Their legacy was two ideas: virtue is enough for happiness, and most social conventions are optional.
Few people would want to live as he did, but his challenge holds up.
How many of our wants are real needs, and how many are what society tells us to want?
Modern minimalism and the urge to declutter echo him.
A simple test: of any possession or ambition, ask whether losing it would leave you truly worse off, or only less admired.
The key idea: Diogenes turned an exile over defaced coins into a motto: challenge the false values society stamps onto things.
Part two. Epicurus: the surprising philosophy of pleasure.
Today 'epicurean' suggests fine wine and rich food.
But Epicurus, the philosopher behind the word, lived simply in a garden, ate bread and water, and taught that the secret of happiness was needing less.
The Garden.
Today 'epicurean' suggests fine dining, but Epicurus lived simply.
Born on the Greek island of Samos in 341 BC, he later bought a house with a garden near Athens, and his followers became known as the Garden.
Ancient sources say it welcomed women and enslaved people, who were usually excluded from philosophical schools.
Members lived simply and valued friendship above all; Epicurus is reported to have called it the greatest thing wisdom provides.
The ancient biographer Diogenes Laertius says Epicurus lived mainly on bread and water, and once asked a friend to send a little pot of cheese so he could have a feast whenever he liked.
Pleasure means calm.
Epicurus held that pleasure is the beginning and end of a happy life.
His enemies, ancient and modern, presented that as an invitation to indulge.
But he defined pleasure in a particular way.
The highest pleasure was a calm state of body and mind: freedom from physical pain, called aponia, and freedom from mental disturbance, called ataraxia.
A banquet might bring a burst of enjoyment, followed by a hangover, debt or jealousy.
A simple meal with friends, eaten without anxiety, could bring deeper and more lasting contentment.
In his Letter to Menoeceus, he says explicitly that by pleasure he does not mean the pleasures of the profligate.
Sorting your desires.
A practical tool at the heart of Epicureanism is a way of sorting desires.
Some are natural and necessary, like food, shelter and friendship.
These are easy to satisfy and bring real peace.
Some are natural but not necessary, like fancy food: fine to enjoy when they come along, but not worth chasing.
A third kind he called empty or vain, like the desire for fame, power or limitless wealth.
These are dangerous because they have no natural limit.
However much you get, there is always more to want, so they breed endless anxiety.
The lesson sounds strikingly modern.
Advertising and social media often work by turning unnecessary desires into what feel like needs.
Nothing to fear.
Epicurus built his ethics on the atomism of Democritus: everything is made of indivisible atoms moving through empty space.
Thunderstorms, earthquakes and disease have natural causes.
He did not deny that gods existed, but argued that perfectly happy beings would not bother to punish or reward humans.
Death was next.
In the Letter to Menoeceus he says death is nothing to us, since good and bad lie in sensation and death ends sensation.
When we exist, death is not present; when death is present, we do not exist.
The Roman poet Lucretius, in On the Nature of Things, added that we do not fear the endless time before we were born, so why fear the time after?
Critics reply that what we dread is losing the good things life would have held.
The fourfold remedy.
Later followers condensed the teaching into the tetrapharmakos, or fourfold remedy, found in the writings of Philodemus.
Commonly translated: don't fear god, don't worry about death, what is good is easy to get, and what is terrible is easy to endure.
The last line reflects Epicurus's view that intense pain tends to be brief while lasting pain is usually bearable, which may seem too optimistic for chronic illness.
Treating philosophy as medicine for the mind echoes modern therapy.
Epicurus also advised 'living unnoticed', away from politics, which he saw as breeding fear and rivalry.
The Stoics and Cicero called this selfish.
Yet Thomas Jefferson called himself an Epicurean late in life.
The question stays fresh: what do you actually need to be content?
The key idea: Around 306 BC Epicurus founded a simple school in a garden near Athens that valued friendship and welcomed women and enslaved people.
Part three. The Socratic method.
The most powerful tool Socrates left us wasn't an answer.
It was a way of asking questions.
Questions, not lectures.
Socrates didn't give lectures.
He asked questions.
He'd find someone confident about a big idea, like justice, courage or piety, and ask them to define it.
Then he'd test the definition against examples until contradictions appeared.
The method is called elenchus, meaning cross-examination or testing.
The aim was not to win an argument but to get closer to the truth.
Socrates said he was just as eager to be refuted as to refute, because being shown a mistake rid him of a false belief, which he saw as a benefit.
He wrote nothing himself.
We know him mainly through Plato and Xenophon, and scholars still debate how much of Plato's 'Socrates' is the real man.
Testing a definition.
At the start of Plato's Republic, the elderly Cephalus suggests that justice means telling the truth and paying back what you owe.
Socrates asks: if a friend lent you a weapon, then went mad and asked for it back, would returning it be just?
Clearly not.
So the definition fails as stated.
Others try new definitions, such as 'helping friends and harming enemies', and each is tested in turn.
Each counterexample forces a better definition.
Often the dialogue ends without a final answer, but everyone understands the question more deeply than before.
Knowing you don't know.
In Plato's Apology, Socrates says his friend Chaerephon asked the Oracle at Delphi whether anyone was wiser than Socrates.
The answer was no.
Puzzled, Socrates questioned politicians, poets and craftsmen.
He found they believed they knew things they didn't.
The craftsmen really did know their trades, but assumed this made them experts on everything else.
He concluded he was wiser in one way only: he didn't think he knew what he didn't know.
This humility is the starting point of the method.
You can't learn what you think you already know.
Midwife of ideas.
In Plato's Theaetetus, Socrates compares himself to a midwife, like his mother.
He didn't implant ideas.
He helped others bring out their own, then checked whether each 'newborn' was sound.
When you reason your way to an insight, you understand it more deeply and remember it longer.
Teachers use Socratic questioning to help students think rather than memorise, and law schools, especially in the United States, use it to grill students about cases.
Many early dialogues end in aporia, or puzzlement.
In the Meno, Socrates questions an enslaved boy about doubling a square's area.
The boy gives a confident wrong answer, sees it's wrong, then finds the right one.
Being shown you don't know is uncomfortable, but it makes you want to find out.
Questions to try.
Useful Socratic questions include: What exactly do you mean?
What's your evidence?
What are you assuming?
Could there be another explanation?
What would follow if that were true?
What would someone who disagrees say?
They work on news stories, workplace decisions and family debates alike.
Cognitive behavioural therapists use similar questions to test anxious thoughts: 'What's the evidence this will go badly?
What would I tell a friend?'
Questioning can feel like an attack if done to score points.
Socrates annoyed powerful Athenians by exposing their ignorance in public, and in 399 BC he was tried and executed.
Used with curiosity, it is a fine tool.
Turn it on your own beliefs first.
The key idea: Socrates questioned confident beliefs to test them, aiming at truth rather than victory.
Part four. Eastern philosophy: sages of India and China.
At the same time Greek philosophy was flourishing, thinkers in India and China were asking similar questions, and reaching different answers.
The Axial Age.

In 1949 the German philosopher Karl Jaspers noticed that in roughly the same period, independent traditions arose that still shape billions of lives: Greek philosophy, the Hebrew prophets, Buddhism and Jainism in India, and Confucianism and Daoism in China.
Some accounts add Zoroastrianism, though its founder's dates are very uncertain.
Jaspers called it the Axial Age, a pivot in human history.
Historians debate how tidy the idea is, and some say it overstates the coincidence.
Still, across the world, thinkers began asking systematically how to live, what makes a good ruler and how to deal with suffering.
Many-sided truth.
Mahavira, Jainism's great teacher, lived in north-eastern India around the time of the Buddha.
Jain thinkers developed anekantavada, or many-sidedness: reality is so complex that any single statement is only partly true.
The parable of the blind men and the elephant illustrates it.
One feels the trunk and says it's a snake, another the leg and says it's a tree.
Each is partly right; none sees the whole.
For Jains, it is a reason for humility and tolerance.
Not all Indian thinkers were spiritual.
The Carvaka, or Lokayata, were materialists.
They trusted only what we perceive directly, so they rejected the soul, rebirth, karma and the gods.
Almost none of their writings survive.
We know them mostly through rivals who quoted them to refute them.
Confucius and his heirs.
Confucius, traditionally dated 551 to 479 BC, was a Chinese teacher and minor official in an age of war between rival states.
He taught ren, humaneness, and li, proper conduct.
Society works when relationships, such as ruler and subject, parent and child, and friends, are carried out with mutual responsibility.
His version of the golden rule, from the Analects: 'Do not do to others what you do not want done to yourself.'
His followers disagreed on human nature.
Mencius held it is basically good: anyone seeing a child about to fall into a well feels compassion.
Xunzi held people are naturally selfish and need education and ritual, as a craftsman straightens wood.
Under the Han dynasty Confucianism became China's state philosophy, and exams on its classics decided government posts until 1905.
Laozi and the Dao.
Daoism is traditionally traced to Laozi, a legendary sage whose historical existence is uncertain, and the short, poetic Dao De Jing, only about 5,000 Chinese characters.
Its opening line says the Dao that can be spoken of is not the eternal Dao.
The Dao, or 'the Way', is the underlying flow of the universe.
Daoism values simplicity, humility and wu wei, often translated as 'effortless action': acting in harmony with things rather than forcing them, like water, which is soft yet wears down stone.
The later sage Zhuangzi famously dreamt he was a butterfly, then wondered whether he was a butterfly dreaming he was Zhuangzi.
Threads and legacy.
Despite big differences, these traditions share threads with each other and with Stoicism.
Many warn that endless desire causes suffering and that compassion is central to a good life.
Buddhism's attention to the mind resembles the Stoic focus on judgements: how we interpret events shapes how we suffer.
Scholars caution against making them sound identical, since their views of the self and universe differ.
Their influence endures.
Confucian values shaped government, education and family life across East Asia for over two thousand years.
Buddhism is practised by hundreds of millions, including many Australians, and its meditation inspired Jon Kabat-Zinn's mindfulness-based stress reduction in the late 1970s.
Daoism shaped Chinese painting, poetry, medicine and tai chi.
The key idea: Between roughly 800 and 200 BC, major philosophical traditions arose independently across several civilisations.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What did Diogenes mean by his motto 'deface the currency'?
Answer. He wanted to challenge society's false values.
Question two. What does Epicurus's own life suggest about the word 'epicurean' today?
Answer. It misleads, as he lived simply among friends.
Question three. What is the point of Socratic questioning?
Answer. To test ideas and get closer to the truth.
Question four. What did Karl Jaspers notice about the period 800 to 200 BC?
Answer. Separate traditions arose in many places.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
